title: The Depth Control and the Split Probe
intro: The level above gave the two controls as two results: a gap of about 17 percent of depth, and a drop from 28 to 6. This level gives them as two procedures. It sets out the mechanism each confound would need in order to be real, how each measurement is actually taken, and how much of the worry each control closes.

chapters.title: What a smuggled answer would look like
chapters.body:
The systematic swap experiment does not intervene on a clean basis. The [[jacobian-lens]] yields one direction per vocabulary token per layer, and those [[j-lens-vector]] directions are neither orthogonal to one another nor of unit length. A [[lens-coordinate-swap]] therefore has to solve for its two coefficients with a pseudoinverse rather than take plain inner products ([[oblique-lens-coordinates]]).

What gets written back into the activation is a whole vector. Nothing in the construction guarantees that the vector for ant is free of a component along the vector for the token 6.

That is the confound. Suppose the lens vector for spider already correlates with the lens vector for 8, and the vector for ant with the vector for 6. Exchanging spider for ant would then push 6 toward the output directly. The model would answer 6 with no intermediate step having been touched at all. From the output side that trial would look exactly like the reasoning result the section claims.

The paper does not try to purify the vectors. It times them instead.

If the intermediate swap acts only through a smuggled answer component, then it and a direct swap of the two answer tokens are one intervention under two names. Two names for one intervention give no reason for either to begin acting before the other.

If instead the model infers the intermediate and then reasons from it, the intermediate has to exist in the network before the answer does. An edit to the intermediate should then have purchase at shallower layers than an edit to the answer.

[[swap-depth-control]] is that comparison. It asks of each swap not whether it works but where it starts to work, and it is aimed at the [[internal-reasoning]] claim in particular. Everything else about the trial is inherited unchanged, including drawing the substitute from the same category as the true intermediate ([[same-category-swap-target]]) and scoring against the answer that substitute implies ([[implied-counterfactual-answer]]).

chapters.title: Where each swap starts to bite
chapters.body:
The headline swap is applied at every layer at once. The depth control cannot be. Getting an onset out of an intervention requires restricting it to a range of layers and then moving the range.

Depth is reported on the paper's usual convention. Results sit on 25 evenly spaced layers of the residual stream, reindexed to run from 0 to 100 ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]). A layer number therefore reads as a percentage of the model's depth rather than as an index into its stack. The median separation of roughly 17 percent is a separation in that unit: about 17 percent of the way through the network, or a little over four of the 25 sampled layers.

The quantity on the vertical axis is the log-probability difference in the expected output. For a swap applied over one range, it is how far that swap moves the log-probability of the answer the substituted concept implies. Where the swap lands too early or too late to matter the curve stays low; where the edit does causal work it rises. The swap runs at single strength throughout, $\alpha = 1$ ([[swap-strength-alpha]]).

The right panel of [[fig-15]] plots the two curves for Sonnet 4.5, with a shaded standard-error band. Two features bear on how much the separation carries.

The average is taken over successful trials only, meaning the trials where the swap moved the implied answer to the top of the distribution. For Sonnet 4.5 that was 70 percent of the 50 items of the [[multihop-benchmark]], the rate that the left panel reports across the [[claude-model-family]] ([[swap-success-rate]]). The curves describe the swaps that worked.

And the control excludes only the strict form of the confound. The two swaps are not one intervention. That is not the same as showing the intermediate's lens vector carries none of the answer. A vector that carried a little of the answer and was also read a step earlier would produce this picture too.

chapters.title: A handle the lens did not build
chapters.body:
The second worry is not about a stray component. It is about the whole instrument. Every result up to this point locates the intermediate with a [[j-lens-readout]] and then intervenes along the same directions. A sceptic can grant every swap and still say that nothing has been shown about the model's own working representation, only about the [[j-space]] the lens happens to single out.

Answering that requires a second representation of the same intermediate, built by another route.

The [[intermediate-probe]] is a mean [[residual-stream]] activation, and the set averaged over is the design. Every prompt in the set implies the same intermediate, China for instance, but through a different surface cue, and each asks a different question about it. Averaging cancels what those prompts do not share: the particular wording, the particular question, the particular answer. What survives is the thing they have in common.

The mean over all intermediates is then subtracted. That removes what is common to the whole prompt family, leaving a direction specific to this intermediate rather than to the format.

A comparison sharpens what the construction buys. The [[concept-vector]] used earlier in the paper is the activation recorded just before the Assistant answers "Tell me about {concept}", mean-subtracted over 100 other concepts. That vector stands for a concept the model has been handed. The intermediate probe stands for one the model had to infer.

Neither construction touches the lens, which is the point. But the probe is a mean-difference direction of the same family as a [[linear-probe]], and it carries the same caveat. It is a correlational read of the activations. That it is the model's working representation of the intermediate, rather than one direction that happens to track it, is an assumption the experiment makes rather than a result it establishes.

chapters.title: Cutting the probe against the lens dictionary
chapters.body:
The split is not a projection onto an orthogonal basis. The lens supplies one vector per vocabulary token per layer, an overcomplete and non-orthogonal dictionary, so an arbitrary activation has no unique decomposition into it ([[sparse-decomposition]]).

[[gradient-pursuit]] resolves that greedily. It selects dictionary elements one at a time and updates the coefficients along gradient directions, stopping at a fixed budget. Here the budget is $k = 25$ vectors and the coefficients are constrained to be nonnegative, so the fit is a sum of lens directions with positive weights, never one direction cancelling another.

Whatever that sum captures is the probe's [[j-space-component]]. The rest of the probe is the remainder, and the remainder is defined by subtraction alone. It is not characterised independently; it is what 25 lens directions failed to reach.

The fit is small. Those 25 vectors typically account for roughly 10 to 15 percent of the probe's variance, which is to say that 85 to 90 percent of what distinguishes this intermediate's mean activation from the others is not reconstructable from any nonnegative combination of them. That sits with the paper's general finding that an activation's J-space component never exceeds about 10 percent of total variance.

Greediness has a cost the paper records. Because the decomposition is not unique, the pursuit can settle on a near-miss correlate of a concept that is still forming across layers rather than on the concept's own vector. That is noise in what the component is later said to name.

The same cut was made earlier on concept vectors, in the report experiment of [[fig-8]] ([[j-space-privilege-for-report]]), where the component held a median of 6 to 7 percent of the variance. [[j-space-component-decomposition]] is one design run twice: once on a concept the model was given, once on a concept it inferred.

chapters.title: Four conditions and the clamp
chapters.body:
The scoring set is 90 two-hop prompts, larger than the 50 the depth panel used. On it the raw lens swap reaches the implied answer on 60 percent of trials rather than the 70 percent Sonnet 4.5 scored on the smaller set, so the two figures are not directly comparable numbers for the same quantity.

The bars of [[fig-16]] carry [[wilson-interval]] error bars, the Wilson score interval for a proportion, which is used because a normal approximation behaves badly for rates near the ends of the scale. At $n = 90$ those intervals are wide enough that 60 and 61 percent cannot be told apart. That is what the comparison wants: the claim is that the small J-space component matches the instrument it was built to check, not that it beats it.

The gap that carries weight is 61 against 28.

Then the clamp. A remainder swap that flips 28 percent of answers admits two readings. The remainder may drive the output on its own. Or the perturbation may cause downstream layers to re-derive the intermediate and write it back into the J-space, which then drives the output.

[[complement-clamped-swap-control]] separates them by closing the route back in. The intermediate's J-space coordinates are held at their clean-pass values at every position and every layer ([[activation-clamping]]). A footnote fixes which coordinates those are: the tokens making up the probe's J-space component, plus the token that directly names the concept if it is not already among them. The rate falls to 6 percent, and the same control drove the remainder's effect to zero in the report experiment ([[j-space-mediation-clamp]], [[non-j-space-residual-effect]]).

The clamp is itself a heavy intervention, held for a whole forward pass. The section reports no separate measurement of what clamping alone costs on these prompts.
chapters.childScope: Take the scoring of [[fig-16]] condition by condition: what each of the four swaps writes into the activation, why 61 percent for the [[j-space-component]] against 60 for the raw [[lens-coordinate-swap]] is read as a match under [[wilson-interval]] bars, and how [[complement-clamped-swap-control]] with [[activation-clamping]] distinguishes the two readings of the remainder's 28 percent ([[non-j-space-residual-effect]]).
